title: Shelach: go and see (Numbers 13:1–2)
hook: twelve scouts are sent to see the land

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses prayed five words for Miriam, and a whole people waited for her. Your line was short prayers count. Today, a new portion, at the edge of the land.

Before you sign a lease, you visit the apartment. You open the closets, run the shower, check whether the windows face a brick wall. Before a big move, people drive through the new town at night to see if it's quiet. Nobody wants to commit to a place sight unseen. The Israelites are camped in the wilderness of Paran, at the edge of the promised land. The next step is to walk in. And first, someone wants a look around.
screen: `VISIT BEFORE YOU SIGN.` → `AT THE EDGE OF THE LAND.` → `FIRST, A LOOK AROUND.`

segments.voice: God says to Moses: "Send thou men, that they may spy out the land of Canaan". In Hebrew, shelach lecha: send for yourself. That extra word, lecha, caught Rashi's eye. He reads it as permission, not command: send if you want to; I'm not ordering it. Why put it that way? Because in Deuteronomy, Moses remembers that the people asked for it. They wanted a report first. So twelve men go, one leader from each tribe. One of them, Hoshea, gets a new name from Moses: Yehoshua, Joshua. Moses gives them a careful list of questions. See the land, what it is. The people living there: strong or weak, few or many. The cities: open camps or fortified. The soil: rich or poor. Are there trees? Be of good courage, he says, and bring back some of its fruit. It was the season of the first ripe grapes. They go for forty days, from the south to the far north. Past Hebron, in a valley later called Eshcol, cluster, they cut a single bunch of grapes so heavy that two men carry it between them on a pole. Pomegranates and figs too. The verb for their mission, latur, means to scout, to explore, to go around and look. Looking isn't the problem. Moses asked them to see, and to bring back something real. What they do with what they saw, as we'll find, is the test.
screen: `SHELACH LECHA: SEND FOR YOURSELF.` · `TWELVE SCOUTS, ONE PER TRIBE.` · `MOSES' LIST: SEE WHAT IT IS.` · `A CLUSTER CARRIED BY TWO.` · then, large: `GO AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've formed an opinion about secondhand, a neighborhood, a coworker, a book you've only heard about, and notice where the opinion came from: a review, a rumor? Then picture going to see for yourself, and ask Moses' first question: what is it, really?
Shelach. Send: the portion where twelve scouts go to see the land, and bring back a cluster of grapes too big for one man.
Your line: go and see. Seeing for yourself is a good instinct. That's day four hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Shelach is read in synagogue in the yearly Torah cycle; the image of two scouts carrying a giant grape cluster on a pole is a familiar one in Jewish art, and the story of the scouts is studied as a lesson in how people see and report.
